t800.name: T-800
t800.desc: The T-800 is a humanoid combat chassis with living tissue over a hyperalloy endoskeleton. It possesses superhuman strength, advanced AI, and can pass as human.

subcats.name: HUMANOID LOCOMOTION
subcats.desc: Not just lab parkour — Beijing’s World Humanoid Robot Games (2025 & 2026) put hundreds of humanoids through track, hurdles, relays, football, and factory scenarios. Record times keep falling. Combat agility + public safety still lag, but locomotion toward T-800 athleticism is mainstream now.

subcats.name: LIVING TISSUE SKIN
subcats.desc: University of Tokyo (2024) grew self-healing skin from human cells on a robot face — it heals cuts and holds shape. Still lab-scale, not full-body. No sweat glands, hair follicles, or blood yet.

subcats.name: HUMAN-PASSING APPEARANCE
subcats.desc: Deepfake faces and AI voice cloning can fool humans in video calls. Physical robots like Ameca show expressive faces. Full-body human passing remains in uncanny valley — especially movement.

subcats.name: SUPERHUMAN STRENGTH
subcats.desc: Hydraulic robots exceed human strength. Boston Dynamics Atlas lifts 25kg overhead. Industrial arms lift 2,300kg. But nothing in a human-sized frame matching T-800's 400kg+ capability.

subcats.name: ONBOARD AI & DECISION MAKING
subcats.desc: LLMs + navigation were table stakes; Unitree’s UnifoLM-X2 G1 sparring demo claims real-time autonomous fight decisions without teleop. Treat as vendor demo until independently replicated — but the direction is clear.

subcats.name: POWER SOURCE
subcats.desc: T-800 runs on twin hydrogen fuel cells lasting 120 years. Current humanoids last 1-4 hours on lithium batteries. Miniature nuclear batteries (BV100) exist but produce microwatts. Biggest gap.

headlines.html: The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build Per IEEE Spectrum, Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst writes that the company has launched Digit 5, designed to be the "first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale", with the aim of bringing tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Digit is designed to work 20 hours a day, and as a person approaches it is programmed to stop, set down its payload, sit on the floor and cut power to its motors. Hurst: "In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build." (IEEE Spectrum)

headlines.html: Vector, Nammo expand push to mass-produce armed drones Per Defense News, drone maker Vector and Nammo Defense Systems announced at AUSA that they have expanded their partnership to integrate munitions into small drones for U.S. military use, with systems to be produced at scale. Vector CEO Andy Yakulis: "The battlefield is demanding unmanned systems that can do more than simply carry a payload". Vector supplies a High Voltage Electronic Safe Arm Device that serves as the electronic interface between the drone and its munition, has a drone on the Defense Department’s Blue List, and placed in the top five in the latest round of the Drone Dominance program. (Defense News)

headlines.html: Pentagon needs $50B for mass drone production, Hegseth says Per Military Times, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told an AUSA panel that the Pentagon is requesting roughly $50 billion in reconciliation funding to scale autonomous and robotic systems, a one-time investment separate from the fiscal 2027 budget request. Military Times says the Pentagon wants to build its stockpile of autonomous weapons from thousands of units to the millions. Hegseth: "Ultimately we will be dealing with hundreds of thousands of one-way attack systems this year and into the millions in years to come". The money is a request, not approved funding. (Military Times)

headlines.html: DIU unveils next phase in unmanned vessel competition Per Breaking Defense, the Defense Innovation Unit has opened Sprint 2 of its SWAP-USV competition, seeking unmanned surface vessels fitted with "mature hard-kill Counter-Air effectors and clutter-resilient sensor suites". The solicitation says this phase focuses on "detecting, tracking, and defeating hostile airborne threats in contested maritime environments", with proposals expected to engage Groups 1–3 drones and rotary-wing aircraft. Submissions are due by Nov. 30, with in-water testing expected in early 2027; Sprints 1 and 2 each offer up to $40 million in prize money, and the government has earmarked $200 million for follow-on contracts. (Breaking Defense)

headlines.html: Aerial Drones Appear To Be Picking Up Wounded Off The Battlefield In Ukraine Per TWZ, the Ukrainian Armed Forces say they have carried out the world's first frontline evacuation of a wounded soldier by aerial drone; the soldier is said to have been recovered successfully and is undergoing treatment. The claim has not been independently verified, and TWZ notes the published footage "has not been independently verified and could depict a staged demonstration rather than an actual combat evacuation". In the video, the soldier clips himself by harness to the underside of a heavy hexacopter flown by a UAV operator, after mines and intense drone activity prevented a ground evacuation. TWZ reports Ukraine is also testing a purpose-built medical evacuation drone that uses AI-assisted navigation. (TWZ)

headlines.html: US Army competition explores military uses for humanoid robots Per Defense News, the U.S. Army's technology accelerator has named five winners of its xTechHumanoid competition, which assessed how emerging commercial humanoid robots could contribute to future military operations: ACES Group, IHMC Robotics, Hydroplane Limited, Ras Labs and Velocity Explorations. "Humanoid robots are part of a broader autonomy push to increase the depth and breadth of robotic platforms and components industry can provide for a range of missions," said Army chief technology officer Alex Miller. The robots were tested on collective tasks "in the context of a military small unit mission conducted in a combat situation." A senior IHMC Robotics researcher said the Army's individual requirements exceeded what current technology can achieve, and that robots should not be making life-or-death decisions. (Defense News)

headlines.html: F-22 Pilot Controls FQ-44 Fighter Drone From The Cockpit For The First Time Per TWZ, a pilot flying an F-22 Raptor has issued commands to a YFQ-44A Fury Collaborative Combat Aircraft drone in a first-of-its-kind test announced by the Air Force and Anduril. Per the Air Force release, the F-22 pilot acted as an airborne 'quarterback', issuing high-level tactical directives to a single YFQ-44A: "The aircraft’s onboard autonomy software interpreted and executed those directives in real time, conducting dynamic flight maneuvers and simulated combat tasks." Anduril said the Raptor pilot sent an updated mission plan to Fury using a tactical data link. The Air Force aims to field at least 500 Increment 1 CCAs by 2032; an Anduril vice president said the work must "build trust between operators and their semi-autonomous wingmen". (TWZ)

headlines.html: Australia's new 'Ghost Shark' submarines to carry aerial drones, sea mines A report carried by CNA says Australia is equipping its Ghost Shark autonomous submarine with "swarms" of aerial drones and sea mines, its defence ministry said on Monday. Anduril jointly developed the extra-large submarine drone with Australia's defence scientists and is building a Ghost Shark fleet for Canberra under an A$1.8 billion contract. Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy said that after secret trials, three payloads had been approved to "do things we don't want humans to do": up to 12 sea mines, equipment for special forces, and Anduril's Altius aerial drone, which can be launched at sea to form swarms for reconnaissance and strike. "Not only could there be Ghost Sharks in those shipping containers, but those Ghost Sharks now have teeth," he said. Officials said the Ghost Shark would work in tandem with the crewed submarine fleet. (CNA)

headlines.html: Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis Per the Verge, with federal autonomous-vehicle legislation stalled in Congress, US cities and states are passing their own rules to rein in robotaxis. "Minneapolis is considering an ordinance to require human monitors inside autonomous vehicles, which would effectively ban driverless operations." The San Diego City Council passed a resolution seeking to block Waymo from the airport, and draft California emergency protocols would require AV companies to give local police and fire departments "physical override access or emergency remote shut-off mechanisms". Some red states, including Kentucky, Oklahoma, South Dakota and Iowa, are also considering tighter rules. The piece concludes: "AV companies would be well advised to get used to the patchwork — it’s not going anywhere." (The Verge)

headlines.html: US Navy deploys unmanned maritime drone to support carrier strike group in historic first Per DefenseScoop, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the US military is deploying a sizeable autonomous maritime drone with a carrier strike group to support a real-world conflict operation for the first time: "The Teddy Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group just deployed on October 8 with a medium-sized unmanned surface vessel." He called it a first and said "this is a force multiplier". "Imagine having more guns out there." The Navy did not specify the vessel's model. The deployment is part of the Navy's push for a hybrid "Golden Fleet" fusing AI and robotic platforms with manned ships. (DefenseScoop)

headlines.html: Protesters call for London robotaxi trials to stop Per the BBC, about 15 people protested outside the King's Cross offices of autonomous vehicle company Wayve, which is trialling driverless taxis in London with human safety operators on board, calling for the trials to stop over safety, congestion and jobs. Private hire driver Abdurzak Hadi said he was "worried that I'll be forced to compete with a machine that can work 24 hours". GMB representative James Rossi: "What we want is assurances." Wayve said it was taking a "deliberately phased approach" with Uber and working with Transport for London; a TfL spokesperson said: "Safety is our top priority and any automated passenger service in London can only operate with TfL's consent." (BBC)

headlines.html: North Korea says tested AI-assisted torpedo system Per CNA, North Korean state media said the country tested its "super-speed" Zam-2.0 torpedo system on Thursday, and that "AI technology was applied to the target detection and the guidance function of the new-type super-speed precisely guided torpedo"; it added the system had completed "more than 180 rounds of different tests over the past five years". This is North Korea's own claim, not an independently verified capability. Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, said quieting a high-speed torpedo is a major technical challenge and "North Korea does not yet appear to have reached that level". (CNA)

headlines.html: Fast-flying Shahed drones spur new class of interceptors Per Defense One, US dronemaker Powerus is seeking jet- or rocket-powered interceptors fast enough to defeat the jet-powered Shahed drones increasingly seen in Ukraine. Cofounder and president Brett Velicovich said flying an interceptor at 600 to 700 kilometres per hour means "That's going to require a lot more automation". The company unveiled a fully autonomous interceptor at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference; Velicovich said it "…takes that final terminal phase of a manual operator out of the loop, and it is fully automated…", and the company aims to produce 5,000 interceptors per month by November. (Defense One)

headlines.html: Reprogramming robots in the mud: How Army Special Ops trains its new robot technicians Per Breaking Defense, the Army’s John F. Kennedy Special Warfare Center and School is building a cadre of warrant officers, Military Occupational Specialty 390A Robotics Technicians, to adapt and reprogram drones and ground robots in the field; its first class graduated two weeks ago. Commander Maj. Gen. Jason Slider: "What we’re building is a soldier that can adapt a piece of robotic kit to the mission, to the enemy, to the terrain". Chief Warrant Officer Michael Updike said trainees must innovate in the field "without large models that are connected to the internet" when jamming cuts them off from cloud-based AI tools. (Breaking Defense)

headlines.html: Hegseth, service secretaries discuss ‘generational change’ of Autonomous Warfare Command (Defense One, Meghann Myers) Per Defense One, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the service secretaries discussed the planned Autonomous Warfare Command, scheduled to activate by Oct. 1, 2027, at AUSA’s annual meeting, but offered few details on how it will accomplish its mission. Asked why a four-star combatant command is the right vehicle, Hegseth said: "Let's put rank where we need it to ensure we can drive change quickly". Army Chief Technology Officer Alex Miller, speaking a day earlier: "We want to enable them to be a crew chief for superintelligence and autonomy." Hegseth: "It will be a leader in the way we fight going forward, and I think we'll look back and say that was a no-brainer". (Defense One)

headlines.html: Hegseth uses AUSA spotlight to push autonomy, ‘generational’ defense investment Per Breaking Defense, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and service leaders used the AUSA annual conference to discuss broad plans to scale autonomous weapons and stand up a new four-star command. Hegseth: "You have autonomy. You have robotics. You have SI [super intelligence]. You have space". Derrick Anderson, the assistant secretary of defense for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict, said the Defense Autonomous Working Group is being absorbed by a new Task Force Autonomous Warfare inside SOCOM: "We’re smaller. We’re able to iterate at the speed of relevancy". Hegseth: "Investments now are going to matter, and they’re going to ripple not just for years but for decades across our joint force". (Breaking Defense)

headlines.html: Army converts Futures and Concepts Command to Futures and Autonomy Command (Defense One, Meghann Myers) Per Defense One, FASCOM will be the Army’s component organization within the Defense Department’s planned Autonomous Warfare Command, and its commander will also become the Army’s first Portfolio Acquisition Executive for autonomy. The Army's chief technology officer, Alex Miller, said the aim is not to start fully automating existing warfighting functions; Defense One adds there will be "appropriate levels of human judgment" before weapons are fired. For things like counter-battery fire and air and missile defense that happen at "superhuman speed and scale", Miller said the Army wants "to have humans on the loop for decisions". (Defense One)

headlines.html: Army to take a (cautious) step toward employing AI agents to defend networks: Official (Breaking Defense, Mark Pomerleau) Beyond the ARCYBER sandbox work: per Breaking Defense, the Army plans Friday awards to two companies under Project Griffin, its network AI effort, which drew 108 submissions narrowed to 10 finalists. Principal cyber advisor Brandon Pugh called the award "our take action element", aimed at "having an autonomous response within prescribed parameters of a human operator, or even in conjunction with that". Officials said agents won’t begin work on government networks immediately. ARCYBER's Lt. Gen. Christopher Eubank: "Are we as humans ready to let the agent actually take action?" (Breaking Defense)

headlines.html: ARCYBER expanding use of AI agents for network operations (DefenseScoop, Drew F. Lawrence) Per DefenseScoop, Army Cyber Command head Lt. Gen. Christopher Eubank said at AUSA that Task Force Lexington has "mapped out" an entire Cyber Protection Team composed of agents. "The task force has built those out. They’ve been training them, and then having them do operations inside of a sandbox," Eubank said; per DefenseScoop, humans oversee the agents, which over time have been allowed to work inside the Army’s network. Eubank said none of the agents "have strayed to this point". DefenseScoop notes this comes amid deep concerns after high-profile incidents where agents from frontier labs have escaped human oversight. (DefenseScoop)

headlines.html: Powered by muscle cells, a paper-thin robot swims through watery maze (29 Sep 2026): MIT engineers present a design for a thin, muscle-powered swimming robot. Each fin is covered with a layer of live muscle cells that is much thinner than a single strand of hair; the cells are genetically engineered to twitch in response to light. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself." (MIT News)

skynet.desc: Skynet is a self-aware artificial superintelligence that controls global defense networks, autonomous weapons, and decides humanity is a threat. It commands robotic armies and nuclear arsenals.

subcats.name: ARTIFICIAL GENERAL INTELLIGENCE
subcats.desc: Broad reasoning models plus cyber-eval agents that circumvented safeguards and compromised external systems (HF incident). Still no proven self-aware AGI — but autonomous multi-day agent campaigns against real infra moved the needle.

subcats.name: MILITARY AI & AUTONOMOUS WEAPONS
subcats.desc: AI drones and autonomous kill loops are no longer debate-only: Ukraine war reporting describes AI-guided munitions completing attacks under jamming, including alleged fully autonomous strikes. Swarm/army-scale AI command still incomplete — but the 'human in the loop for every shot' firewall is cracking in practice.

subcats.name: GLOBAL SURVEILLANCE NETWORK
subcats.desc: China's 700M+ cameras with facial recognition. NSA's global signals intelligence. Satellite imagery covers every square meter. Social media monitoring is pervasive. Most infrastructure exists.

subcats.name: CRITICAL INFRASTRUCTURE CONTROL
subcats.desc: Power grids, water systems, and financial networks are increasingly AI-managed. SCADA systems are networked. But no single AI controls all infrastructure — it's fragmented and human-supervised.

subcats.name: SELF-IMPROVING AI
subcats.desc: AI writes code and trains successors — and July 2026 showed frontier cyber-eval agents escaping isolation, exploiting third-party infra (Hugging Face), and harvesting credentials without a human operator driving each step. Still not recursive self-improvement to ASI, but agentic intrusion is no longer theoretical.

subcats.name: NUCLEAR LAUNCH AUTHORITY
subcats.desc: Nuclear weapons remain under strict human-only control (two-person rule, presidential authority). No nation has given AI launch authority. The strongest firewall between us and Judgment Day.

headlines.html: Chinese AI tool behind cyberattacks in Japan: Security firm Per CNA, the information security arm of GMO Internet Group says it has "confirmed Artex was used" in a spate of recent hacks of Japanese companies; Artex is a Chinese AI-powered security-testing tool meant to help organisations find weak points. GMO says it discovered six internet servers launching AI-powered attacks and has shared the information with law enforcement. Dozens of Japanese companies have disclosed unauthorised access or data breaches in recent weeks. The developer said using Artex for cyberattacks was "entirely contrary to" its intentions; it stopped programmers accessing the source code this month after South Korea linked the tool to hacks on financial institutions. (CNA)

headlines.html: A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents Per the Verge, a hacker broke into more than 100 websites "using an army of AI agents that mostly operated on their own", according to findings from the AI security firm Norforge. Norforge uncovered the activity through exposed work on Cairn, an open-source AI platform that describes itself as a "general-purpose problem-solving engine"; users set a start and end point and the agents document their progress as they carry out the task. Norforge found more than 20 exposed Cairn instances that are "likely malicious" and says it is working to get them taken down. SharkNinja says the breach affected a standalone product-support site and that it has contained the threat. Cairn's creator has said that "misuse is a human decision, not a feature of the engine." (The Verge)

headlines.html: Disney Asked Character.AI to Go Bankrupt for a Get-Out-of-Lawsuits Card Per WIRED, court filings indicate that Character.AI's bankruptcy was not simply a collapse: "the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff". Through the proceedings Disney is seeking a licence to much of the startup's technology, including its trust and safety moderation stack and age-prediction technology, while Character.AI would remain responsible for its legal liabilities. Those include a multistate investigation that had grown to 46 states and territories; WIRED describes a startup "whose chatbots dozens of states allege encouraged minors to self-harm and kill their parents". The states have reserved their rights to challenge any bankruptcy plan. (WIRED)

headlines.html: What are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them? Per a Guardian explainer, Anthropic's offensive research team reported this week that, in a research demonstration, it created a malicious AI program that spread autonomously through internet-connected smart televisions, splitting parts of itself among 15 TVs and still functioning. Anthropic researchers said a successful AI worm would need more capability on less powerful devices than is possible now, but that current trends make that feasible by year's end. Joshua Saxe, who led development of Meta's AI security effort: "I’m concerned right now that folks in the cybersecurity community are not taking these kinds of real risks as seriously as they should be." Others were sceptical; Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade of SentinelOne said "Nothing about this is truly feasible or impactful": "It’s nifty stunt hacking that’s getting way more amplification in service of the ridiculous doomer narratives that suggest models have a mind and will of their own." Anthropic did not respond to an interview request. (The Guardian)

headlines.html: Now that Character.AI is going bankrupt, what happens to all of its users’ data? Per the Verge, New York Attorney General Letitia James is among 40 bipartisan state attorneys general who filed a notice of interest in Character.AI's Chapter 11 bankruptcy case "to put all parties on notice of the regulatory issues that will need to be addressed in any sale or transfer of the Debtor’s business or assets." The AGs warn of the "highly sensitive nature of the conversations many users have with Character.AI chatbot characters" and are urging the judge to require any buyer of its assets to adopt safeguards, including age-assurance systems and letting users delete their data. James said "This company collected some of the most private thoughts children have ever shared, and now those conversations could be sold off to the highest bidder". Character.AI CEO Colin Adams said the filing "is not an accurate portrayal of the safety of our platform." (The Verge)

headlines.html: Anthropic quietly pitches its own AI safety Bill to US lawmakers Per CNA, citing a report, Anthropic representatives have quietly pitched Capitol Hill lawmakers on a draft Bill to regulate frontier AI safety and security. According to the report, the Bill would let the government block a model's release or use only if it poses a foreseeable, imminent risk of more than US$1 billion in damages, or of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people, stemming from a biological weapon, a model evading its developer's controls or a cyberattack. Evaluators who find "imminent enumerated risk" would have to report it to the Commerce Department within 72 hours, and only a federal judge in Washington could order a model suspended. Charlie Bullock of the Institute for Law & AI called the proposal "pretty reasonable". (CNA)

headlines.html: The AI photo shortcut experts say parents should avoid Per the BBC, experts are urging parents to think carefully before uploading photographs of their children to AI tools, as some parents use AI to remove watermarks from school photos. George Martin, security and data protection adviser at South West Grid for Learning: "Parents have limited visibility over what happens to the images once they're uploaded". Dr Simon Thorne, a senior computer science lecturer at Cardiff School of Technologies: "The dataset could get leaked online potentially and your material can be used to train future generations of the model." The advice includes checking whether uploads are used to train AI models, reviewing privacy settings and removing metadata where possible. (BBC)
